# Be Excellent Where You Are

[Silas Bambil · October 2026]{.meta}

I once came across an observation that resonated with me so much that I made it my X header: “When you give your best at work, you do yourself the bigger favour than your company. And remember, how you do anything is how you’ll do everything. Excellence compounds, the more you do excellent work, the more you get used to doing excellent work. Be excellent where you are!” What particularly appealed to me about those words was the idea that the benefits of doing something well extend beyond the thing itself. Every opportunity to exercise excellence is also an opportunity to develop the person who will undertake the next task.

I wake up every day wanting to become a better version of myself. I want to know more than I knew yesterday, understand things that previously confused me, and become capable of doing things that once appeared beyond my abilities. There is something immensely satisfying about returning to a problem I once found difficult and discovering that I now understand it. The problem has not become any easier; I have simply become better equipped to deal with it. I genuinely enjoy that experience, and much of my enthusiasm for learning comes from knowing that there are still so many things I cannot do today that I might eventually learn to do.

Perhaps this explains why my interests have continued to expand throughout my education. I studied actuarial science and subsequently pursued further education in quantitative risk analysis, statistics, and related disciplines. Along the way, I have pursued professional qualifications and developed interests in subjects that were not necessarily part of my original academic ambitions. Although I appreciate the qualifications I have acquired, some of the most meaningful returns on my education are things no institution could have printed on a certificate. I do not merely want to possess qualifications that suggest I am knowledgeable. I want to possess the knowledge those qualifications are supposed to represent.

My growing interest in research has given me another opportunity to experience this kind of development. I enjoy investigating problems concerning credit risk, extreme events, statistical methods, and uncertainty. What fascinates me is how much I discover in the process of trying to understand something. Sometimes, revisiting an analysis reveals weaknesses I had previously overlooked. An apparently convincing result may require me to reconsider my assumptions, while a question I thought I had answered may expose several others I had not considered. Although correcting my own work can be frustrating, I find considerable satisfaction in recognising that I have become capable of identifying problems I would previously have missed.

I experience something similar when developing statistical software. Getting a programme to work is satisfying, but I also want to understand why it works, whether its results are correct, and under what circumstances it might fail. I want to produce something another person can use with reasonable confidence. Sometimes, achieving that requires revisiting work I had initially considered complete. What makes the effort worthwhile is that, throughout the process, I become better at programming, statistical reasoning, and solving problems. A research manuscript or a piece of software may remain unpublished, but I do not finish working on it as quite the same person who began it.

Having spent considerable time studying finance and mathematics, I find the idea of compounding particularly fascinating when applied to personal development. Everything meaningful I learn becomes part of the knowledge available to me when I encounter another problem. The discipline I develop while undertaking one difficult task can influence how I approach the next. A mistake I understand today may prevent several others in the future. What excites me is that these improvements do not necessarily remain independent of one another. The knowledge, abilities, and judgement I accumulate can complement each other in ways I cannot always anticipate. I genuinely believe that my excellence will compound.

Admittedly, there have been occasions when I have questioned where all this effort is taking me. I have invested years in my education and professional development, yet I have experienced considerable difficulty securing the employment opportunities I had hoped for. I would be lying if I said that did not sometimes frustrate me. I want my abilities to translate into meaningful professional opportunities, financial independence, and a comfortable life. Nevertheless, I try not to confuse the absence of an immediate reward with the absence of personal development. There are days when my circumstances appear no different from how they were yesterday, even though I may have become a little more capable.

I also try not to make my satisfaction with personal development entirely dependent on how well I compare with other people. There will always be people who know more than I do, possess greater experience, or have accomplished things I have yet to accomplish. I enjoy encountering such people because they often make me aware of how much more there is to learn. However, I would find it unfortunate if their achievements prevented me from appreciating my own development. I want to retain the ability to celebrate becoming better at something without first needing to establish whether I am better at it than somebody else.

More importantly, I do not want becoming a better version of myself to mean becoming only a better statistician, researcher, programmer, or finance professional. I want to become a better son, brother, cousin, friend, and, someday, a good husband and father. I want to become more patient, more considerate, and more willing to acknowledge when I have behaved poorly. I would find it rather disappointing to spend decades acquiring knowledge and developing impressive professional abilities while making very little progress in how I treat the people I love. Surely, the person I am becoming ought to be reflected in more than the things I can put on my CV.

Part of pursuing excellence, for me, involves becoming increasingly comfortable with discovering that I am not yet as good at something as I might have imagined. There are weaknesses in my abilities, shortcomings in my character, and aspects of my behaviour that I would genuinely like to improve. I do not always enjoy having these things brought to my attention, but I recognise their importance. I cannot reasonably expect to become a better person while continually defending everything about the person I currently am. I hope that becoming more knowledgeable will make me increasingly curious about what I do not know rather than increasingly convinced of my own superiority.

I am also learning to appreciate that pursuing excellence does not require me to accomplish something remarkable every day. There will be days when I am tired, discouraged, or simply unable to do as much as I would have liked. There will be occasions when resting is a more sensible decision than insisting on continuing with something. I do not want my enthusiasm for personal development to become a source of unnecessary anxiety or make me incapable of enjoying the person I already am. I want to pursue excellence because I genuinely enjoy becoming better, not because I believe that every unproductive day diminishes my worth.

What I particularly love about the expression “Be excellent where you are” is that it does not require me to wait until my circumstances become ideal. I do not have to secure my preferred job, publish a manuscript, complete another degree, or become financially comfortable before deciding to take personal development seriously. There are things I can learn and abilities I can develop within my present circumstances. Giving something my best does not mean that I must accept unreasonable demands from others or continually exhaust myself. It means that I do not want the difference between where I am and where I hope to be to become an excuse for neglecting what I am capable of doing today.

I do not know precisely where all these years of learning, research, professional development, and personal growth will eventually take me. I do not know which of the things I am currently learning will become particularly useful or what opportunities will allow me to demonstrate what I have become capable of doing. Nevertheless, I find the prospect of discovering who I might become genuinely exciting. Perhaps, years from now, I will find myself capable of doing something that the person I am today cannot even imagine, and much of what makes it possible will have accumulated on rather ordinary days. I look forward to discovering what all that excellence will have compounded into.

**Be excellent where you are!**
